newsitem.title: PERU: Police turn back hordes of relatives in Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Police turn back hordes of relatives in Peru crisis.

text.p: Massed police turned back scores of relatives trying to bring food, medicine and clothing to their loved ones on Friday in the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, calling for order.
The flood of relatives jostling police lines in the streets outside the elegant residence was so great that authorities refused to keep taking supplies, directing them instead to the Red Cross.

"We are only trying to get water and clothing to them. They (the hostages) have let us know they are uncomfortable," said Antonio Zelada, whose father was one of about 400 hostages, including high-ranking foreign diplomats, businessmen and government officials.

Hostages expressed their desperation by displaying hand- written signs at a second-floor window in various languages pleading for water, electricity and telephones to be reconnected and food to be brought.

Their lives hung in the balance as President Alberto Fujimori's government took a hard line against the rebels' demand to free jailed comrades, and there was no sign of a breakthrough in negotiations.
"The only thing we want is that there are no victims," said Rosa Alva, who was released along with the other women late Tuesday hours after the spectacular assault.
Other relatives of hostages begged local media to avoid provoking the rebels by calling them "criminals" or terrorists", tags commonly used here.
"Every one of them (the rebels) is heavily armed with equipment in backpacks," Alva said.

"We want everybody to remain calm and for the press not to insult them," said Mariela Molina, whose brother had spoken to her from within the residence to say the rebels were treating their captives well.
Ordinary citizens, like an 11-year-old girl from the Indian highland town of Ayachucho phoned, radio stations to say they were praying for the safety of the hostages.
Red and white Peruvian flags were draped from windows or hoisted from makeshift masts all over the country to show solidarity with the government against the rebels.
At the height of Peru's 16-year guerrilla conflict in the late 1980s few Peruvians dared display the national flag for fear of being attacked.

Human rights groups were organising a gathering near the siege for Friday evening. They called on the public to urge a peaceful solution by wearing white clothing, and carrying white flags and candles.
